items.title: Claude Code Computer: Anthropic just launched Computer PTC Feature & IT'S INSANE!
items.summary:
In this video, I'll be telling you about Anthropic's new Programmatic Tool Calling capability, or PTC, and how it's changing the way agents handle multi-step tasks while using fewer tokens and delivering better results.

--
Key Takeaways:

🧠 Anthropic introduced Programmatic Tool Calling (PTC), a new capability available in Claude Opus and Sonnet 4.6.
⚡ PTC lets Claude write code that orchestrates multiple tool calls inside a container, reducing round-trip overhead.
📉 PTC improved accuracy by 11% on average while using 24% fewer input tokens across benchmarks.
🏆 Opus 4.6 with PTC is currently ranked number one on LMArena's Search Arena benchmark.
🔧 PTC is now built into the web search tool on the API by default, so you get the benefits automatically.
🔄 You still keep full control through tool handlers for logging, inspection, and human approval.
👍 Overall, PTC gives you the best of both worlds: the composability of code and the control surface of tools.
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: Hi, welcome to another video. So, Anthropic team recently published an article about something called programmatic tool calling or PTC. And this is a really interesting capability that's available in Claude Opus and Sonnet 4.6. It basically changes how agents handle multi-step tasks like search. and it recently helped Opus 4.6 score number one on Elmarina's search benchmark. I read through the whole thing and I want to break it down for you because this is quite important to understand. So, let's get right into it. First, let's talk about how tools work right now. When you use the API, you can give Claude tools by specifying a tool name, description, and input arguments. When Claude wants to use a tool, it responds with a JSON object, a tool handler runs it, and the result gets passed back into Claude's context. If you run this in a loop, you basically have an agent. The bash tool is a great example. Claude generates a command like pip install requests. It gets executed and the result comes back. Now the article starts with a really important question. Computer use is one of Claude's most central capabilities and just giving Claude a bash tool opens up a really broad action space. So the question becomes, is bash all you need? And how do you decide what other tools to give an agent? Claude with a bash tool running in a loop is essentially a computer use agent. This is how claude code works at its core. But claude code doesn't just use bash. It uses tools as a control surface around certain actions. And the article explains when it makes sense to promote an action to a dedicated tool. First is UX. Some actions need to be caught and rendered to the user in a specific way like the ask user question tool in clawed code. Second is guard rails. For example, a file edit tool can run a staleness check to make sure the file hasn't changed since the model last read. Third is concurrency control. Read only tools can run in parallel, so grouping them makes sense. Fourth is observability. You might want to isolate specific actions for logging like measuring latency or token usage. And fifth is autonomy. You may want to group actions by autonomy level. If the harness can undo an action, it can approve it more freely. So tools give you a lot of control. But here's the problem, and this is the core insight of the article. Tools trade off control with composibility. Consider three actions as tool calls. The context from each tool call is returned back to Claude. Each round trip costs latency, serializes the full tool result into context, even if the next step only needs a tiny part of it, and introduces a reasoning step. So you could have thousands of rows coming back when the next step only needs five. And you're paying this composition tax for every single tool call. The more actions you chain, the worse it gets, which is really not ideal. And this is where programmatic tool calling comes in. The article describes PTC as a capability that unites the composibility of code with the control surface of tools. So with PTC, you still define your tools as usual, but instead of Claude calling them one by one, Claude writes code that orchestrates multiple tool calls inside a code execution container. When the code calls a tool like await web search with a query, the container pauses. The call crosses the sandbox boundary as a typed tool use event. It gets fulfilled just like a normal tool call through your handler or an MCP server. But here's the key difference. The result returns to the running code, not to Claude's context window. The code then processes the result following whatever control flow Claude specified. It can call another tool, filter the data, accumulate results, do whatever it needs to do programmatically, and only the final processed output reaches Claude's context. So all the intermediate stuff stays inside the container and never bloat up Claude's context. This is pretty amazing to be honest. Now let's talk about the results. With Opus 4.6, they've seen significant gains in both token efficiency and performance. For example, instead of pulling 50 raw search results into context for Claude to reason over, the code can parse, filter, and cross reference results programmatically. It keeps what's relevant and throws away the rest through dynamic filtering. And the numbers back this up. Across browse comp and deep search QA benchmarks. PTC improved accuracy by an average of 11% while using 24% fewer input tokens. So you're getting better results while spending less. And Opus 4.6 six with PTC is currently number one on LM Arena's search arena which is just amazing because of these gains. PTC is now built into the web search tool on the API by default. So when you use the web search tool with Opus 4.6, you automatically get the benefits of PTC for better performance and token savings. You just pass the web search tool type in your API call and PTC handles the rest behind the scenes which makes it super easy to get started with. Now the really clever part about this whole approach and this is what makes PTC different from just using code execution is that you get the composability of code while still keeping the control surface of tools. The tool handlers still sit in the middle of every call. They can inspect, reject, log, or cue actions for human approval. But Claude can fluently orchestrate all these actions in code instead of doing them one at a time. So you get the best of both worlds. So to summarize the whole thing, the traditional tool calling approach gives you control but kills composability because of the roundtrip tax. PTC solves this by letting Claude write code that orchestrates tools inside a container, keeping intermediate results out of context and only returning the final output. You still get all the control of tool handlers for inspection, logging, and approval, but now Claude can chain actions efficiently through code. Overall, this is a really solid improvement to how agents handle multi-step tasks. If you're building agents or using the API, I definitely recommend checking out PTC and the new web search tool. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, share your thoughts below and subscribe to the channel. You can also donate via super thanks option or join the channel as well and get some perks. I'll see you in the next video. Bye.

items.title: Claude Code (New Updates): New SIMPLIFY & BATCH Skill Agents, Better UX, New Commands & MORE!
items.summary:
In this video, I'll be telling you about the latest Claude Code updates, including two brand new skills, slash simplify and slash batch, that could completely change how you handle code quality and large-scale migrations.

--
Key Takeaways:

📋 AskUserQuestion can now render markdown previews, so you can see diagrams and code snippets before making a choice.
📋 The new slash copy command instantly copies Claude's last response to your clipboard, saving you time every day.
🔗 HTTP hook handlers let you connect Claude Code to external services, databases, CI pipelines, and custom security policies.
🚀 Slash simplify uses parallel agents to automatically improve code quality, efficiency, and CLAUDE.md compliance.
⚡ Slash batch runs large-scale code migrations in parallel using git worktrees, with each agent handling its own isolated chunk.
🛠️ Slash batch works best for conflict-free migrations like Jest to Vite, CommonJS to ES Modules, or Solid to React.
👍 Overall, these updates make Claude C
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: Hi, welcome to another video. So, Claude Code just got a bunch of new updates and some of them are actually really useful. There are four main things I want to cover today, including two brand new skills that I think a lot of you are going to love. So, let's get right into it. First up, the ask user question tool can now show markdown snippets. Now, if you've used claude code before, you know that when it needs your input, it asks you a multiplechoice question like which layout should the config panel use and it gives you options like compact, spacious, sidebar, and so on. Previously, you just see the text labels and pick one. But now it can actually render markdown previews right next to each option. So for example, if Claude code is asking you to choose a layout, it can show you an actual ACI diagram of what each layout looks like. You can see the sidebar with settings categories on the left, the form fields on the right, all rendered right there in the terminal. This is pretty great because before you were basically guessing what each option meant. Now you can see diagrams, code snippets, configuration examples, all of it before you make a choice. It's a small change, but it makes a big difference when you're making architectural decisions. Next, there's a new /copy command. This one is simple, but super handy. When you type /copy, it copies the last message from Claude directly to your clipboard. So, let's say Claude just generated a code block or gave you an explanation. Instead of manually selecting everything, scrolling through a long response, and trying to copy it all, you just type /copy and it's done. It even tells you how many characters and lines were copied. No more messing around with terminal selection. If you use claude code daily, this is going to save you a lot of small annoyances. Now, this next one is pretty great for developers who want more control over their workflow. They've added a new HTTP hook handler. So, Claude Code already had hooks, which let you run custom logic before or after certain tool calls. But before this update, hooks were limited to running local shell commands. Now you can point your hooks to HTTP endpoints. So in your settings.json, you set up a pre-tool use hook, give it a matcher like bash and then instead of running a shell script, you point it to an HTTP URL. You can set a timeout, add authorization headers with bearer tokens, and even reference environment variables using the allowed envir field. So, for example, you could have a hook that posts to localhost 8,800/hooks/p pre-tool use every time cla to run a bash command. This is actually really powerful because it means you can now integrate cloud code with external services. You could have a server that validates commands before they run, logs everything to a database, triggers CI pipelines, or even applies custom security policies. If you're working in a team environment and want to enforce certain rules about what Claude Code can and cannot do, this is exactly how you'd set that up. The docs for this are already live on code.claude.com/doccks/n/hooks if you want to check it out. And finally, the biggest additions in this update, two brand new skills, slashsimplify and/batch. These were announced by Boris Churnney from the Claude Code team, and honestly, they both sound really impressive. Let's start with /simplify. This skill uses parallel agents to improve code quality, tune code efficiency, and ensure claude.md compliance. So the way you use it is you make your code change first and then you tell claude to run /simplify. It spins up multiple agents running in parallel. Each one looking at different aspects of your code. One might be checking for code quality issues. Another might be tuning performance. And another might be making sure everything lines up with your claude.md configuration. Think of it as an automated code review that doesn't just flag problems, it actually fixes them. And because it uses parallel agents, it's fast. You can even chain it with other commands. Like you could say, "Hey Claude, make this code change, then run /simplify, and it'll do both in sequence." If you're someone who cares about shipping clean code, this is going to be a daily tool for sure. Now, slashbatch is the one I'm personally most excited about. This skill is designed for code migrations, and it works at scale. You interactively plan out a migration with Claude, define what needs to change, and then it executes the work in parallel using dozens of agents. Each agent runs with full isolation using git work trees. So every agent gets its own copy of the repo, makes its changes, tests everything, and then puts up a PR. So if you need to migrate from just to vite across your entire codebase, you just run /batch migrate from justest to vite. Claude will figure out which files need to change, split the work across multiple agents, and each one handles its own chunk independently. Same thing if you're migrating from Solid to React or converting CommonJS to ES modules or any other parallelizable refactor. Now, there is one thing to keep in mind. Slashbatch is designed for tasks that don't have conflicts. Each sub aent gets its own folder or set of files to migrate. If two agents need to touch the same file, you'll need to ask the main agent to resolve those conflicts manually. But for the vast majority of migrations where each component or module can be updated independently, this is going to save hours of work, maybe even days on larger code bases. Combined, these two skills automate a lot of the tedious work that used to go into shephering a pull request to production and performing large scale code migrations. Before this, you'd have to manually go file by file, test each change, and hope you didn't miss anything. Now, Claude Code handles all of that in parallel with proper isolation and testing. Overall, these are some really solid updates. The /simplify and/batch skills alone could change how a lot of people work with cloud code on bigger projects. The HTTP hooks open up a whole new world of integrations for teams. And even the smaller additions like /copy and the markdown previews and ask user question just make the day-to-day experience smoother. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, share your thoughts below and subscribe to the channel. You can also donate via super thanks option or join the channel as well and get some perks. I'll see you in the next video. Bye.
